Apportionment: How a Count Becomes Seats

Why the Constitution orders a census, the six rules that turn it into seats, and what happens when the margin is smaller than the instrument

When the Census Bureau published the 2020 apportionment of the House of Representatives, the 435th and last seat went to Minnesota. The state that would otherwise have taken it was New York, and the distance between them was 89 people.

89 people is a large lecture hall. Because the count fell the way it did, New York holds one fewer vote on every bill that passes the House for a decade. It casts one fewer vote for President in two elections, and stands one place further back in every federal formula that pays out by seat.

Dividing 435 seats among 50 states will essentially never come out in whole numbers, and the way the final allocation is settled will benefit some state while costing another. States sue over it. NCSL’s Redistricting Law 2020 summarises the census cases that have reached the Supreme Court, and two of them are fights over a seat. Department of Commerce v. U.S. House of Representatives (1999) turned on whether the Bureau could use sampling to apportion. Utah v. Evans (2002) was about a seat that had already moved from Utah to North Carolina.

Why the Constitution orders a count

The census is not a survey that happens to be used for apportionment. It is the other way around. A national headcount exists because of a single clause about seats. Everything else the count now does came afterwards: the funding formulas, the redistricting files, the whole statistical apparatus built on top.

Article I, Section 2 says that Representatives “shall be apportioned among the several States which may be included within this Union, according to their respective Numbers.” In the next breath it orders the count that makes that possible: “The actual Enumeration shall be made … within every subsequent Term of ten Years, in such Manner as they shall by Law direct.”

The clause is there because the Constitutional Convention had deadlocked on it. One camp wanted the states represented equally, one wanted them represented by population, and the compromise gave the Senate to the first and the House to the second. A House built on population needs a recurring headcount or it is not built on population at all — it is built on whatever anyone believed about population in 1787, forever. The decennial census is the mechanism that keeps the House attached to the country. It is a constitutional obligation with a deadline, not a statistical program with a purpose.

Two amendments to the rule matter. The original clause counted “three fifths of all other Persons,” which gave slaveholding states representation for people they did not represent. The Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2, replaced that with “the whole number of persons in each State, excluding Indians not taxed.”

The Constitution also fixes exactly two numbers. Every state gets at least one Representative. No state gets more than one per thirty thousand people, which is a ceiling on the size of the House, not a floor.

Between those two bounds the Constitution says nothing at all. It does not say how many Representatives there should be, and it does not say how to round. That second silence is the subject of this chapter, and it has been contested for longer than almost anything else in American public law.

A seat is three things at once

Before the rounding, be precise about what is being divided. A seat is a vote on legislation. It is an elector in the Electoral College. And it is a unit of the formula by which a large share of federal money is distributed. The arithmetic therefore does not merely describe representation; it produces it.

Two disputes run alongside it, and they are different. The first is which method. Adams’s, Dean’s, Webster’s, Jefferson’s, Hamilton’s and Huntington–Hill are all defensible and they do not agree. Congress has changed its mind five times and settled on the current rule in 1941. In Department of Commerce v. Montana (1992) the Supreme Court declined to second-guess that choice, holding that Congress had acted within its constitutional authority.

The second is how many seats. The number 435 is not in the Constitution. It has been fixed by statute since the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929. The House grew with the country for a hundred and forty years, and then stopped.

Fifty rows, and a column that is not what its name says

The file that settles all of this has one row per state and four numbers that matter.

State People living there Counted from abroad Apportionment population Seats
California 39,538,223 38,534 39,576,757 52

Read the middle column slowly. The apportionment population is not the population of the state. Federal employees serving overseas, mostly military, are counted and then assigned back to a home state. That assignment is a policy decision rather than a measurement. It is a small column, and it is not the same kind of thing as the one beside it.

Fifty rows, not fifty-one: the District of Columbia has no apportioned Representative and does not appear.

One producer, one deadline

Almost every file in this book was made by somebody for a purpose other than the one it is being put to here. This one was not. Title 13 of the U.S. Code obliges the Secretary of Commerce to report the apportionment counts to the President within nine months of Census Day. The President transmits them to Congress, and the Clerk of the House then tells each state how many Representatives it has.

The obligation is the whole reason the file exists. It also explains the one thing about it that looks like carelessness. The 2020 results were due at the end of 2020 and arrived in April 2021, because the pandemic had disrupted the count and the Bureau chose lateness over a number it could not defend. A file with a statutory deadline records the deadline being missed rather than quietly interpolating.

That deadline is also why the file is unlike almost any other in this book. The 435 seats in it are not a measurement of how many seats the states have; they are how many seats the states have. Nothing stands between the number and the thing.

The difficulty is one rung down, in the population. “How many people lived in Minnesota on 1 April 2020” sounds like a fact awaiting collection, and it is not quite one. Somebody has to decide where a college student is in their second year, where a prisoner is, where a family halfway through a move is, and where a soldier stationed in Germany is. Each of those is a residence rule, written in advance, that could defensibly have been written another way.

The last of them is visible in the file as its own column: 348,698 people nationally were counted abroad and assigned back to a home state, and this chapter returns to what that does. The rest of the rules are invisible, because they were applied before the count was tabulated and no column records them.

The tables sit at fixed public addresses on the Bureau’s own server, so anyone who doubts a number in this chapter can fetch the file again and check it. Everything done to those 50 rows from here on is arithmetic: a different rounding rule, a larger House, the seat New York did not get.

Rounding sounds like the absence of a rule

The obvious way to divide the House is to work out each state’s fair share of it, its quota, and round.

State Apportionment population Fair share of 435 Seats
California 39,576,757 51.99 52
Texas 29,183,290 38.34 38
Florida 21,570,527 28.34 28
New York 20,215,751 26.56 26
Pennsylvania 13,011,844 17.09 17
Illinois 12,822,739 16.85 17

New York’s fair share is 26.56 seats. It cannot have 0.56 of a seat, so somebody must decide which way that goes. Round to the nearest whole seat and the total comes out at 435 — exactly right.

That is luck, not design. Nothing forces the fractions to cancel.

The total is right. The House is not.

State Fair share Seats if we round Seats actually held
New York 26.559 27 26
Ohio 15.514 16 15
Rhode Island 1.443 1 2
Montana 1.426 1 2

4 seats sit in different states. Rounding gives one each to New York and Ohio and takes one each from Rhode Island and Montana.

This is a direction, not an artifact. Large states have large fractions to round up; small states have small ones. “Round to the nearest whole seat” sounds like the absence of a rule and behaves like a policy.

There is also a floor. Three states are not entitled to a full seat at all:

State Apportionment population Fair share Seats
Alaska 736,081 0.967 1
Vermont 643,503 0.845 1
Wyoming 577,719 0.759 1

The Constitution guarantees each state at least one Representative, so Wyoming’s 0.76 of a seat becomes a whole one. Somebody else gives that up.

The floor is only half of it. Three other states hold exactly one seat while being entitled to more than one:

State Apportionment population Fair share Seats
Delaware 990,837 1.302 1
South Dakota 887,770 1.166 1
North Dakota 779,702 1.024 1

Six states hold one seat. Three are owed less than a seat and get one anyway; three are owed more than one and get one anyway. Delaware and Wyoming send the same number of Representatives, and Delaware has 1.72 times the people. One Delaware Representative answers to 990,837; one from Wyoming answers to 577,719.

Neither is a mistake. The floor is in the Constitution and the rounding is in the statute. Between them they open that gap before Huntington-Hill hands out a single contested seat.

Every seat is bought at a price

Huntington–Hill gives every state one seat, then hands out the remaining 385 one at a time. Before each handout, every state posts a bid, called its priority value, and the highest bid takes the seat. For a state’s kkth seat the bid is

priority=populationk(k−1)\text{priority} \;=\; \frac{\text{population}}{\sqrt{k(k-1)}}

and that is the whole method. There is nothing else in it.

The formula in action

Work the first one by hand. Every state already holds one seat, so every state is bidding for its second, and k=2k = 2 for all of them. The divisor is 2×1=1.41421\sqrt{2 \times 1} = 1.41421, which is the same for everybody, so the first contested seat simply goes to the largest state:

California:39,576,7572×1=39,576,7571.41421=27,984,993\text{California:}\quad \frac{39,576,757}{\sqrt{2 \times 1}} \;=\; \frac{39,576,757}{1.41421} \;=\; 27,984,993

No other state can post a higher number, so seat 51 is California’s. That much is obvious, and it is worth stating precisely because the next step is where people’s intuition breaks.

Does California take seat 52 as well? It is by far the largest state; its population has not changed. But the divisor has. California now holds two seats, so it is bidding for a third, k=3k = 3, and its bid falls to 39,576,757 ÷ 3×2\sqrt{3 \times 2} = 16,157,143. Texas is still bidding for its second at a divisor of 1.41421, which puts it at 20,635,702.

Texas takes seat 52. California comes back for seat 53. Winning lowers your own next bid, which is the entire reason the queue self-corrects rather than handing the whole House to California.

These are the Bureau’s own published priority values, from the table it releases alongside the results. Apply the formula above to the population column and it reproduces every one of them to the last digit.

The table runs to House seat 445, ten seats past the 435 the statute allows. So the queue behind the last seat is not a counterfactual anybody has to construct: the Bureau published it.

Watching the queue empty

Every seat is bought at a price, and because winning lowers the winner’s next bid, the price only ever falls.

Drag the slider. Each tread is one seat, drawn at the price the winning state paid for it. The line never rises, because winning lowers the winner’s own next bid. The dotted line is the price of seat 435, the level New York had to reach and did not; the shaded band past it is the ten further seats the Bureau published priority values for and the statute does not allow.

Figure 1. The price of a seat, seat by seat, as the queue empties. Each tread is one seat, drawn in the order it was won, at the priority value of the state that took it. Seat 51 went to California at a priority of 27,984,993; seat 435 went to Minnesota at 762,998, a fall of about 37-fold. The line never rises: winning a seat lowers a state’s priority for the next one, so the queue self-corrects. The staircase carries on into the shaded band, where the Bureau’s table runs to seat 445 and the statute does not follow — the open circle is the seat New York would have taken.

Check Result
Seats handed out one at a time 385
Total when the queue empties 435
Does this reproduce the official House, state for state? TRUE
Do the recomputed prices match the Bureau’s published ones? TRUE

It reproduces the House exactly. There is no committee and no fudge factor. Once the census is counted, the House allocates itself.

Short by 89

89 people. Had they been counted, the House of Representatives and the Electoral College would have been different for ten years. That margin is the number everyone quotes about the 2020 census, and it is almost always quoted to argue that the count needs to be more accurate.

Before you read on, write down two numbers. First: how close was the second state in line — the one that would have taken seat 437, had there been one? Second: New York’s apportionment population includes people counted overseas and assigned back to the state by rule. How many, next to a margin of 89?

The queue behind New York

Second place first.

New York 762994 89
Ohio 762258 11,462
Texas 758071 189,645

Each dot is how many more residents a state needed for one additional seat. The scale is logarithmic, so a dot rather than a bar: bar length on a log axis would encode the distance from an arbitrary origin rather than the quantity. These are the eight states nearest a further seat, ordered by how short they fell; New York is about 129 times closer than the next of them.

Figure 3. How far every near-miss state was from one more seat. The eight states closest to a further seat, ordered by how short they fell; each dot is the number of additional residents that state needed. The scale is logarithmic, so a dot rather than a bar — bar length on a log axis would encode distance from an arbitrary origin rather than the quantity. New York is the red dot at 89. The next state, Ohio, is about 129 times further away.

Most readers guess that second place was also close — a few thousand, perhaps tens of thousands. It is 11,462, about 129 times the margin that decided the seat. New York’s near-miss was not the normal state of affairs; it was a freak event, and the distance to second place is the evidence. Nothing about the 2020 apportionment was generally knife-edged. One comparison out of 50 happened to be.

Then the second number.

Quantity People
New York’s population counted from overseas 14,502
Minnesota’s population counted from overseas 3,258
The margin that decided the 435th seat 89

New York had 14,502 people counted from abroad — about 163 times the margin. A rule about where to assign soldiers stationed in Germany moved a hundred and sixty times more people than the count difference that settled the seat. Change that rule and you change the House, without changing a single person’s whereabouts.

So the obvious reading is wrong. 89 people is not evidence that the census needs to be counted more carefully. It is evidence that the margin fell below the resolution of the instrument — below the census’s own published uncertainty about state totals, and far below a policy choice already sitting inside the number. “Count harder” is not a strategy here. There is no recount for a census, and the thing that would have to be recounted has an administrative rule inside it that is 163 times larger than the quantity in dispute.

Six rules, six different Houses

Everything so far has assumed Huntington–Hill. Congress did not have to choose it, and for most of American history it did not.

Five of the six named methods are the same queue with a different answer to one question: at what point between kk seats and k+1k+1 does a state deserve the next one? Put that crossing point in the divisor and the rest of the machinery never changes.

Method The divisor for a state’s next seat Who it favours
Adams k — the smallest possible, so every fraction rounds up small states
Dean the harmonic mean of k and k+1 — which comes to making each state’s district as close to the ideal size as it can be, counted in people small states
Huntington-Hill the geometric mean of k and k+1: √(k(k+1)) — the same aim, counted in percentages rather than in people small states, slightly
Webster k + 0.5 — the arithmetic mean, which is ordinary rounding neither, on average
Jefferson k + 1 — the largest possible, so every fraction rounds down large states
Hamilton not a divisor at all: whole shares first, then the largest fractions neither

Hamilton’s is the odd one out, and it is the one people invent on their own. Give every state the whole number part of its fair share, then hand the leftover seats to whichever states have the largest fractions. It is the method the first Congress passed, and it is the method that will fail later in this chapter in a way none of the others can.

Run all six on the same census, at the same 435 seats, with the same one-seat floor. 21 states hold a different number of seats depending only on which rule is used:

State Seats under Huntington-Hill Adams Dean Webster Jefferson Hamilton

Texas 38 -1 · · +2 ·

New York 26 · · +1 +2 +1

Read a column as “what this rule would do to the official House.” Adams moves 5 seats, Jefferson 9, and they move them in opposite directions: Jefferson takes seats off small states and gives them to California, Texas and Florida; Adams does precisely the reverse. That is not a coincidence about 2020. A divisor of k+1k+1 always makes a state wait longer for its next seat, which costs a state with few seats proportionally more; a divisor of kk always lets it in early.

Two of the six break their own promise:

Method States given more or fewer seats than their fair share allows
Adams California, Texas, Florida
Dean none
Huntington-Hill none
Webster none
Jefferson California, Texas, New York
Hamilton none

A state’s fair share of 435 seats is a number with a fraction in it, and the least a method can promise is to land on one of the two whole numbers beside it. Jefferson gives California, Texas and New York more seats than the whole number above their fair share. Adams gives the same three states fewer than the whole number below it. Hold on to that: it is half of a theorem at the end of this chapter.

Change the rule, change the House

Pick a rule, then drag the size. Every seat is recomputed from the fifty apportionment populations while you watch; nothing here is precomputed. With Huntington–Hill selected the comparison is against the official House of 435, so the list shows what growing the House alone would do. With any other rule selected the comparison is against Huntington–Hill at the same size, so the list shows what changing the rule alone would do.

Figure 4. What each rule would do to the official House. Blue is a seat gained, red a seat lost, against the 435 seats actually allocated. Only the 21 states that move under some rule are shown; the other 29 hold the same number under all six. Every column is the same census, the same one-seat floor and the same 435 seats. Only the crossing point differs.

Two things in that table are worth sitting with. Webster’s method is the plain rounding from the start of this chapter. A divisor of k+0.5k + 0.5 is exactly rounding at the half. So the obvious approach anybody would invent turns out to be one of the named contenders, and Congress adopted it in 1842.

Huntington–Hill differs from Webster only by using the geometric mean of kk and k+1k+1 instead of the arithmetic mean. The geometric mean is always slightly smaller, which lets a state in slightly earlier, which is worth slightly more to a state with few seats than to one with many. That microscopic difference is the whole of what protects Rhode Island and Montana.

Under Dean’s method the chapter’s opening sentence changes entirely: the 435th seat leaves Minnesota and goes to Idaho, and New York still does not get it.

Two centuries of arguing about the rule

The choice has never been technical, and the country has fought about it from the beginning.

1792: the first veto in American history was about rounding. The first Congress passed an apportionment bill using Hamilton’s method, taking whole shares first and then the largest fractions, and set the House at 120 by dividing the national count by 30,000. Washington’s cabinet split, with Jefferson and Attorney General Randolph against the bill and Hamilton and Knox for it, and on 5 April 1792 Washington vetoed it.

His two objections were arithmetic. No single divisor applied to the state populations produced the numbers in the bill, and the bill gave eight states more than one Representative per thirty thousand people, which the Constitution forbids. The House failed to override. Nine days later Washington signed a replacement using Jefferson’s method, a divisor of 33,000, and a House of 105. The first exercise of the veto power was a dispute about how to round.

1832: the method starts losing arguments it cannot answer. Jefferson’s method gave New York 40 seats on a fair share of 38.59 — more than the whole number above its quota, the same failure the table above records for 2020. John Quincy Adams and Daniel Webster each proposed rules that could not do that. Congress switched to Webster’s method in 1842, and to Hamilton’s in 1852.

1876: a presidential election turned on it. The 1872 apportionment did not follow any declared method; Congress simply added nine seats. Rutherford Hayes beat Samuel Tilden in the Electoral College by 185 to 184. Balinski and Young (2001) later showed that had the seats been apportioned by Hamilton’s method, the method then on the books, Tilden would have been President.

1880: the arithmetic produces something nobody thought possible. C. W. Seaton, chief clerk of the Census Office, computed the apportionment under Hamilton’s method for every House size from 275 to 350. He found that Alabama received eight seats in a House of 299 and seven in a House of 300. Adding a seat to the House took one away from a state. The next section shows that this is still true of the 2020 file.

1920: Congress simply declined to run the arithmetic. The count had shown a country that had become urban and foreign-born, and the sitting rural majority declined to give up its seats. Ten years passed with a House that did not reflect the census — the only time in American history that reapportionment failed to happen.

1929 and 1941: the two statutes still in force. The Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929 froze the House at 435 and made reapportionment automatic, so that a future Congress could not repeat 1920 by inaction. Twelve years later, after two National Academy of Sciences panels, Congress fixed the method of equal proportions by statute. It was not a disinterested choice. Under Webster’s method the 1940 census gave Arkansas six seats and Michigan eighteen; under Huntington–Hill it gave Arkansas seven and Michigan seventeen. A Democratic Congress moved a seat from a Republican state to a Democratic one and then made the rule permanent, and it has run every apportionment since.

The Alabama paradox is still in the file

Hamilton’s method is the one most people invent when asked. It has an obvious defence: nobody gets more or fewer seats than the whole numbers beside their fair share. It also has one catastrophic property. Enlarging the House can take a seat away from a state.

This is not a nineteenth-century curiosity about a dataset nobody has. Run Hamilton’s method on the 2020 apportionment populations, growing the House one seat at a time, and it happens 30 times between 400 and 700 seats — including, still, to Alabama:

Growing the House from Costs this state a seat It drops from While these two gain
493 to 494 seats Alabama 8 to 7 Texas and Washington
414 to 415 seats Connecticut 5 to 4 California and Texas
422 to 423 seats Wisconsin 8 to 7 California and Florida
436 to 437 seats Rhode Island 2 to 1 Texas and Florida
447 to 448 seats Rhode Island 2 to 1 California and Texas
459 to 460 seats Montana 2 to 1 Texas and North Carolina

Look at the first row. A House of 493 seats gives Alabama 8. A House of 494 seats, one seat larger with nobody’s population changed by a single person, gives Alabama 7. The extra seat goes to Texas and Washington, and Alabama pays for it.

Nothing has gone wrong in the arithmetic. Alabama’s fair share rose, as everybody’s did. It simply rose more slowly than two other states’ fractions, and Hamilton’s method hands seats to whoever holds the largest fraction when the music stops.

Alabama’s seat count as the House grows, on the 2020 apportionment populations. At 493 seats Alabama holds 8 under Hamilton’s method; at 494 it holds 7, with nobody’s population changed. Huntington–Hill cannot do this to any state, at any size, ever.

Figure 5. Adding a seat to the House takes one away from Alabama. Alabama’s seat count under Hamilton’s method and under Huntington–Hill, as the total size of the House runs from 479 to 508. The red line falls at 494. The pale blue band beneath it is Huntington–Hill, drawn wide because the two rules agree everywhere else. It cannot fall anywhere. Every divisor method can only ever move a state’s seat count upward as the House grows, because growing the House simply adds another round to a queue that has already run.

That is the trade. Hamilton’s method never violates a state’s fair share and can take a seat away when the House grows. Huntington–Hill can violate a fair share, though it does not happen to in 2020, and can never take a seat away when the House grows. There is no rule that does both, and the next section is about why.

No method satisfies everything

The two failures this chapter has shown are not accidents of the 2020 file, and they are not fixable. Balinski and Young proved that no apportionment rule can avoid both.

  • Staying within quota means never giving a state more or fewer seats than its fair share rounded either way. Jefferson’s and Adams’s methods fail this on the 2020 census; Hamilton’s cannot fail it, ever.
  • Avoiding population paradoxes means that growing the House, or a state growing faster than another, can never cost a state a seat. Every divisor method — including Huntington–Hill — passes this by construction. Hamilton’s fails it, and Alabama is the name it got in 1880.

Their theorem is that those two are incompatible: any rule that always stays within quota must sometimes produce a paradox, and any rule that never produces a paradox must sometimes leave quota. The choice is between which failure you prefer, and Balinski and Young argue that the method Congress chose systematically favours small states over large ones.

The courts have declined to arbitrate. In Department of Commerce v. Montana the Supreme Court unanimously upheld the method of equal proportions after Montana lost a seat under the 1990 census, holding that the choice among defensible methods belongs to Congress. Utah v. Evans (2002) turned on a seat decided by a comparably tiny margin, where the Bureau’s use of “hot-deck imputation” shifted a seat from Utah to North Carolina. The Court again upheld the Bureau. There is no judicial remedy for being on the wrong side of a close apportionment.

And the arithmetic only runs when Congress lets it. The answer to “does the arithmetic decide?” is no. Congress does. The arithmetic decides once Congress agrees to run it, and 1920 is the decade that proves it: the seats were never reapportioned at all. The 1929 statute that finally settled the matter also froze the House at 435, where it remains while the country has more than tripled.

Apportionment is not a House problem

That impossibility is not a quirk of the American rule. The word names a general problem, not an American institution: divide a fixed number of indivisible things among claimants, in proportion to some measured quantity. Wherever that problem appears, the same short list of rules appears with it, and so do the same paradoxes.

It appears immediately downstream of the House. A state’s electors are its House seats plus two, so the rule that seats the House also apportions the Electoral College, which is the shortest explanation of why census litigation is partisan. It appears in state legislatures, which apportion their own chambers among counties. It appears in the federal formula grants that pay out per seat or per capita.

And it appears in most of the world’s parliaments under different names. The d’Hondt method, which converts party vote totals into seats across most of Europe and Latin America, is Jefferson’s method with the parties standing where the states stand here. Sainte-Laguë is Webster’s.

Follow this chapter and you have followed the arithmetic of a very large share of the democratic world. What makes the American case worth working is not that the rule is special. It is that the file is unusually clean.

The size of the House is a choice too

Everything above holds 435 fixed. Nothing in the Constitution requires it. That number is a statute, and a statute can be replaced.

The Constitution sets only a ceiling and a floor. No state may hold more than one Representative per thirty thousand people, which at the 2020 count would permit a House of 11,036. Every state must hold at least one. Between those two bounds it says nothing.

Every number the House has ever had came from a statute. The very first amendment Congress proposed to the states, ahead of the Bill of Rights, was a formula for setting the size. It was never ratified and is technically still pending, and the formula it prescribed would today imply a House of several thousand.

What actually happened is simpler. The House grew with the country for a hundred and forty years and then stopped.

Figure 6. The House stopped growing; the districts did not. Seats in the House and people per seat at each census from 1910 to 2020. The House reached 435 in 1913 and has not moved since, while the district behind one seat has grown from 210,328 people to 761,169 — a factor of 3.6. The dashed lines are the two sizes most often proposed.

The inequality between states, and two proposals aimed at it

Districts inside a state have to be nearly equal in population. That is Wesberry v. Sanders and the one-person, one-vote rule that followed it, and it is enforced to within a few hundred people. Districts in different states are under no such rule. The Court has never reached them.

Jeffrey Ladewig and Mathew Jasinski (2008) call the second kind interstate malapportionment, and their argument is that it is now much the larger of the two. After the 2000 census the gap between the largest and the smallest congressional district in the country was 410,012 people. The Court had already struck down a gap of 19,275 people inside Texas, in White v. Weiser, as unconstitutional. The interstate gap was more than twenty-five times larger. On the 2020 file it is 448,133: a seat in Delaware stands for 990,837 people, a seat in Montana for 542,704.

They give it four causes, and a legislature can reach only one of them. State populations are uneven; districts are territorial; the method rounds; and the House has a fixed size. The fourth is the one Congress could change tomorrow, and it is the one they propose changing.

Two proposals for how much bigger recur.

The Wyoming Rule sets the average district no larger than the least populous state, which for 2020 implies about 573 seats.

The cube-root rule is an empirical regularity Rein Taagepera noticed in 1972: national legislatures tend to sit near the cube root of the population they represent. For 2020 that implies about 692 seats, which is what the New York Times editorial board endorsed in 2018 when it argued the House should be expanded, and roughly what Ladewig and Jasinski themselves recommend. The United States sits a long way below the line most other democracies sit on.

Whether either one works depends on what you measure.

Each tick is one state. Adding 138 seats pulls the bulk of the distribution left but leaves the spread almost intact: the largest-to-smallest ratio falls only from 1.83 to 1.76.

Figure 7. 138 more seats move the middle of the distribution and leave the ends where they are. Each tick is one state’s district size; the shaded curves are the distribution of people per seat under a House of 435 and under the 573 seats the Wyoming Rule implies. The bulk shifts left and tightens, which is the part of interstate malapportionment a bigger House does fix. The horizontal bars beneath are the part it does not: the largest-to-smallest ratio falls only from 1.83 to 1.76, and the states at the extremes are not even the same ones.

House size Named Largest district Smallest district Ratio between them
435 in force since 1913 990,837 542,704 1.83
573 Wyoming Rule 779,702 443,885 1.76
692 cube-root rule 643,503 368,040 1.75

Read the last column and the reform looks futile. Adding 257 seats, a House more than half again as large, moves the ratio between the biggest and smallest district from 1.83 to 1.75. Those extremes are produced by the one-seat floor and by where rounding happens to fall, not by the size of the House, which is why they survive almost any change to it.

Run Ladewig and Jasinski’s measure on the same fifty numbers and the reform looks powerful. Theirs sums the squared distance from the national average district across every district in the country. On it, the Wyoming Rule cuts interstate malapportionment by 50 per cent and the cube-root House by 72 per cent.

Neither number is wrong and both come from the same file. A bigger House pulls the bulk of the distribution together and leaves its two ends alone. Which of the two you quote decides whether expansion reads as a remedy or as a gesture, and that choice, not the arithmetic, is where the argument actually happens.

What a larger House would actually change

Two things, and neither of them is equality at the extremes.

The first is the near-miss. A House of 436 gives the seat to New York, and the Bureau’s own priority table names the next nine states after that. The margin this chapter opens with is one statutory seat away from never having existed.

The second is the Electoral College, and it is the larger effect. A state’s electors are its House seats plus two, and that pair is the same for Wyoming as for California. The two senatorial electors are therefore a fixed bonus, and the smaller the House, the larger that fixed bonus looms.

Figure 8. A bigger House dilutes the presidential bonus faster than it equalises districts. Both lines are the same quantity: the weight carried by a resident of the best-served state, divided by the weight carried by a resident of the worst-served. For the House that is the smallest district over the largest. For President it is electors per person, where a state’s electors are its seats plus two. At 435 seats the presidential ratio is 3.81 and the House ratio 1.83; at the 692 seats the cube-root rule implies they are 2.53 and 1.75. Neither line is smooth, because seats are whole numbers and which state sits at each end changes as they are handed out.

The two lines fall for different reasons and at different speeds, and the faster one is the surprise. The presidential ratio starts far higher and drops hard, because the senatorial pair is a fixed bonus and every seat added makes it a smaller share of a state’s electors. The House ratio starts lower and barely moves. Its inequality is not a fixed bonus at all, but the one-seat floor and the rounding, and both of those are still there in a House of a thousand. Expansion is the better tool against the Electoral College’s small-state advantage than against unequal districts — which is close to the reverse of the case usually made for it.

So the honest case for a larger House is not that it equalises districts at the extremes, which it barely does, and not that it fixes the Electoral College, which it only softens. It is that interstate malapportionment across the whole distribution would fall by something like 72 per cent. It is that a Representative would answer to 478,480 people rather than 761,169. It is that a state on the edge of a seat would be on the edge of a smaller one. And it is that 435 is a number chosen in 1929, for a country with less than half as many people in it.

Where the inequality actually is

Figure 7 says how wide the spread is. It does not say where it falls, and the answer is not the one most people expect.

Figure 9. Where a seat is cheap and where it is dear. The first mode shades each state by how far its people-per-seat sits from the national average of 761,169; the second shades by how many more residents it would have needed for one more seat. Alaska and Hawaii are drawn as insets, so their position on the page is a convention rather than a location.

The map does not show what a reader primed by the previous figures expects. The most over-represented state is Montana, at 542,704 people per seat. The most under-represented is Delaware, at 990,837. That is a ratio of 1.83. Both are small states.

The inequality is not big states against small ones. It is produced at the one-seat floor and by where rounding happens to fall, which is why it survives almost any change to the size of the House.

Figure 9 shades the same fifty shapes by how unequal representation is. It says nothing about what the count actually did, which is a different question with a sharper answer: between 2010 and 2020, seven seats moved between thirteen states.

quartz_off_screen 2

Figure 10. What the count moved. Seven seats moved between thirteen states: Texas took two; Colorado, Florida, Montana, North Carolina and Oregon took one each; California, Illinois, Michigan, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania and West Virginia each gave one up. One cell is one seat, and every state is drawn at the larger of its two seat counts. Hovering a state gives its two counts and what a seat cost there; the three keys at the top filter to the states that gained, lost or held. Which cell carries the mark is presentational: a seat is apportioned to a state, not to a place inside it. New York’s falls on Long Island, which sits visually close to Connecticut although it is inside New York.

Set the two maps beside each other and they disagree about what matters. Figure 9 says representation is least equal at the one-seat floor, among states that gained and lost nothing. Figure 10 says the seats that actually moved came off large states in the interior and the Northeast. Neither map is wrong. They measure different things, and a reader who saw only one would walk away with a different account of the same census.

What fifty numbers can testify to

The evidence here is unusually clean and unusually narrow, and both are worth stating without hedging.

It is clean because this is the official file, published by the agency that performed the count, containing the seats that actually exist. It is complete by construction: every state, no sampling, no missing rows, no compilation from sources that disagree.

And it is checkable in the strongest available sense. Running Huntington–Hill from the population column either reproduces the Bureau’s own seat column or it does not, and here it does, state for state. The recomputation matches the Bureau’s published price for every individual seat as well. Very little published political data can be audited that completely.

It is narrow because authority and certainty are different things, and this file has all of the first and not enough of the second. No uncertainty is attached to any number in it. The apportionment population is reported as an exact whole number. The Bureau publishes its coverage error separately, in a different document, on a different schedule, and puts state-level error in the hundreds of thousands, far above 89.

The overseas column is a rule rather than a measurement, recording where the Bureau decided to assign people, and that decision has itself been litigated. It is one decade, so the question of whether some state is always within a few thousand of a seat cannot be settled from it. That would take the 1990, 2000 and 2010 files alongside.

And it says nothing whatever about districts. Apportionment decides how many seats a state gets. Districting decides where the lines go, and the two are confused constantly.

So the sentence this chapter will bear is this. The 2020 House was produced by an algorithm short enough to write out in full, which reproduces the official result exactly, and under it New York missed the 435th seat by 89 people. The sharper version is that 89 is smaller than the overseas adjustment inside New York’s own number by a factor of about 163, and smaller than the runner-up’s shortfall by a factor of about 129. The near-miss is a fact about the rules, not about the accuracy of the count. What this chapter cannot say is that a more careful census would have changed the outcome, because nothing here measures enumeration error and no second source exists against which to check the first.

Three questions stay open, and none of them is settled by a better version of this table. Whether 435 should be the number: the argument that a frozen House is a small-state subsidy compounding every decade is a real one, and this file supports the mechanism without settling the politics. Which method is fairest: Balinski and Young supply criteria, the criteria conflict, and choosing among them is a value judgment wearing technical clothes. And whether apportionment should count residents at all. Evenwel v. Abbott (2016) held that states may draw legislative districts on total population. Attempts to shift the apportionment base to citizens have so far failed, which is not the same as the question being closed.

What is not open is the size of the thing that decided the last seat. It was 89 people, against a rule about soldiers stationed abroad worth 14,502, in a queue where the next state in line was 11,462 away. The instrument does not resolve at that scale, and no amount of counting will make it.

Activity: four states and a jar of pennies

Fifty states are too many to argue about at once. Four are enough to produce the whole argument.

Put nineteen people into four groups of 1, 2, 7, 9. Set 25 pennies on the table between them. Give one instruction: each group should end up with a share of the pennies matching its share of the people. Do not say how.

Every group can work out its own fair number in a minute, and every one of those numbers is defensible. The four numbers will not add up to 25. That is this chapter’s problem, and it arrives before anyone has heard of Huntington or Hill.

Write two numbers down before you touch the figure. How many pennies should the group of 1 get, when its fair share is 1.32? And which group should give one up, so that the four numbers add to 25?

The six rules, without the arithmetic. Every one of them is answering the same question: a group is owed a share with a fraction in it, and somebody has to decide what happens to the fraction.

  • Adams — round every share up. A sliver of a share still earns a whole penny, so the smallest group does best.
  • Dean — make each group’s people-per-penny as close to the average as it can be, measured in people.
  • Huntington–Hill — the same aim, measured in percentages instead of people. This is the one the United States has used since 1941.
  • Webster — ordinary rounding. Above the halfway point a share rounds up, below it rounds down.
  • Jefferson — round every share down. Fractions are simply discarded, which suits the group holding the most pennies already.
  • Hamilton — no rounding rule at all. Hand out the whole shares, then give the leftover pennies to whoever has the largest fractions.

Drag a group, then drag the pennies. All six rules are re-run in the browser on every step; nothing is precomputed. The mandated first penny is on by default, which is what the Constitution does for the states, and at the opening numbers it changes nothing: every group clears one penny on its own. Turn it off and set three groups to 1 against a fourth at 9, with 8 pennies, to see what it is for.

Figure 11. Six rules, four groups, 25 pennies. Each row is one of the six rules from the table above, run over four group sizes instead of fifty state populations. Cells in bold differ from Huntington–Hill, the method in force since 1941: blue is a penny more, red a penny fewer. In the browser the sliders set the four group sizes and the number of pennies. The checkbox decides whether every group is handed one penny before the rules start. All six rules are re-run on every step.

Six rules produce 3 different answers here. Adams’s method gives the smallest group 2 pennies and takes one off the largest. Jefferson’s gives the group of 2 one fewer and hands it to the group of 7. Hamilton’s method agrees with Huntington–Hill at this setting, which it will not do once you start moving the pennies. Nobody has miscounted anything. The group sizes are known exactly, and every bit of the disagreement is about the remainder.

A room full of people makes the same point faster. The largest group reliably invents something close to rounding down, which is Jefferson’s method. The smallest reliably insists that it cannot be left with nothing, which is Huntington–Hill’s guaranteed seat. Both are arguing their own interest, and both are quoting a rule the United States has actually used. Jefferson was Virginia, the largest state in the union. Webster and John Quincy Adams were New England, and New England was small.

Four things to do with it, in the version with the sliders:

  • Make the House bigger and watch a group get smaller. Press set up the paradox, which puts 28 pennies on the table, then move the pennies one step to 29. Group A drops from 2 to 1 under Hamilton’s method. There is more to hand out and one group receives less, which is the Alabama paradox of Figure 5 at four states. The last two rows of the printed figure carry the same two lines.
  • Make the same move under the other five rules. Nothing falls, for the reason given in that section: a divisor method runs a queue, and lengthening a queue cannot take back what it has already handed out.
  • Set all four groups to the same size. Every rule ends up starred, because the last penny is a genuine tie and the answer turns on a coin flip. The exercise is dead at that setting, which is why the numbers it opens on were searched for rather than picked.
  • Turn off the mandated first penny. Set three groups to 1 against a fourth at 9, with 8 pennies. Jefferson’s method gives the large group all eight and the other three nothing. That is what the constitutional floor is for, and it is a floor rather than a property of the rule, because three of these six rules would not impose it on their own.

None of this is a simplified version of the real thing. It is the real thing, with the populations small enough to hold in your head. The rules are the same rules and the failures are the same failures. The reason there is no neutral answer for four groups is the reason there is none for fifty states.

The data itself

Your turn

None of these is answered above, and every one can be answered from the tables you just opened.

  • apportionment_2020.csv has both app_pop and resident_pop, and overseas is the difference. Sort by overseas. Which states gain the most from people stationed abroad, and was any of it enough to move a seat?
  • people_per_seat is not the same in every state. Find the largest and the smallest. How many times over is one person’s share of the House worth another’s?
  • priority_values.csv lists the seats in the order they were handed out. Find the last seat awarded and the first one missed, and see how close the two were.
  • nation.csv goes back to 1910 and carries pop_per_rep. The House stopped growing and the country did not. Follow that column down and say what a fixed 435 has cost.

How the figures were made

apportionment_2020.csv holds the Bureau’s Table 1 and Table 3, and priority_values.csv holds its published priority table. Every number and every figure above is computed from those two files at the moment this document is rendered. The Huntington–Hill queue, all six methods, the Alabama paradox scan, the Wyoming-Rule and cube-root Houses and the Electoral College ratios are run from the population column; nothing is copied from a published summary. The interactive figures ship the same fifty populations to the browser and re-run the same rules there, which is why the seats move while you drag. Figure 11 is the exception, and reads nothing: its four group sizes and its 25 pennies are invented, and the six rules are run over those. The group sizes are the ones the course uses in the room, chosen so that the rules disagree and no penny rests on a tie-break.

counted back into a home state -- which is the difference between the
apportionment population and the resident population. The priority
values workbook is the arithmetic itself: one row per House seat, the
state that took it, which of that state's own seats it was, and the

state rows.

WHAT TO BUILD.
1. A fifty-state table: apportionment population, seats, seat change
   from 2010, and the overseas count folded into each state's total.
2. People per seat, state by state: divide each state's apportionment
   population by its seats, and look at how wide the spread is.
3. The published priority queue as a table, and then the same queue
   recomputed from the population column alone. For a state's kth seat
   the priority value is its population divided by the square root of
   k times k-1. Assign every state one seat, then hand out the rest one
   at a time to whichever state has the highest priority value.
